claims.text: High configurational entropy alone does not guarantee the intrinsic thermal stability of nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal HENA nanoparticles.
HENA stability is governed by kinetic competition between slow diffusion and a thermodynamic driving force for segregation.
The slow-diffusion effect retards phase separation and coarsening in the nanoparticle bulk.
Negative mixing enthalpies and surface-energy minimization provide thermodynamic driving forces for segregation.
Phase separation occurs when the product of atomic-size difference and the magnitude of negative mixing enthalpy exceeds a critical threshold.
Phase separation can produce intermetallic precipitates or elemental segregation.
Segregation should occur preferentially at nanoparticle surfaces because surface energy dominates there.
A high surface-to-volume ratio amplifies surface segregation and reduces the effective activation energy for diffusion.
Nanoparticle surface effects can destabilize a single-phase solid solution at lower temperatures than bulk models predict.
Rapid-quenching routes can synthesize five-component HEA nanoparticles, including CrFeCoNiMo and CrMnFeCoNi-type systems.
Rapid quenching ensures that these nanoparticles initially have a single-phase FCC or BCC solid-solution structure.
The proposed test anneals 10–50 nm particles at 600–1200 K for 1–100 hours under argon or vacuum and then rapidly quenches them.
Configurational entropy stabilizes the solid solution at high temperatures.
Severe lattice distortion and high mixing entropy cause the slow-diffusion effect.
Once thermal energy overcomes the diffusion barrier and the segregation driving force is sufficiently strong, phase separation occurs.
HENAs with atomic-size difference below 6.6% and near-zero or positive mixing enthalpy will remain single phase after annealing at 1000 K for 100 hours.
HENAs with atomic-size difference above 6.6% or significantly negative mixing enthalpy will phase-separate during annealing.
Traditional alloying concepts predict high-temperature solid-solution stability from high mixing entropy and low mixing enthalpy regardless of particle size.
The nanoparticle-specific hypothesis may fail above 100 nm because bulk thermodynamics then dominates.
Comparing high- and low-parameter HENAs after identical annealing is intended to falsify the model if all samples phase-separate or if none do.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires the product of atomic-size difference and mixing-enthalpy magnitude to exceed a threshold, implying a combined criterion, whereas the predicted outcome uses atomic-size difference above 6.6% OR significantly negative mixing enthalpy as independently sufficient.

The hypothesis characterizes traditional bulk stability prediction as based solely on mixing entropy, while the baseline characterizes it as based jointly on high mixing entropy and low mixing enthalpy.
